b: "Is it my resume or is it the market?" is a question I see a lot these days, and it's also one of the first things people ask me on calls. The answer is usually that it's a bit of both, but I think you can get a much better read on it than most people do, and you can do it with some fairly simple math.

So let's start with what a normal interview rate looks like right now. Greenhouse, which is one of the bigger applicant tracking systems out there, published data this fall on about 162 million applications at US companies. Out of every 1,000 applications, 32 made it to a first interview, which works out to roughly 3%.

Huntr, which runs a job tracker, found something pretty similar across close to 2 million applications its users logged. Applications sent with an untailored resume got an interview about 3.1% of the time, and applications sent with a tailored resume got one about 5.7% of the time.

In other words, if you're applying cold, an interview rate somewhere in the 3 to 6% range is about average right now. That may surprise some of you, but it's a big drop from just a few years ago. Ashby found that candidates are about half as likely to get an interview as they were five years ago. These days, not hearing anything back on 20 applications is quite normal.
Even if nothing is wrong with your resume, here's roughly how often you'd still end up with zero interviews, assuming each application has about a 3% chance of turning into one:

If your chance per application is closer to 5%, which is roughly where tailored resumes land, then the chance of getting nothing back from 50 applications drops to about 8%. (This assumes every application has the same chance, which isn't perfectly true, but it's close enough for a ballpark.)

So what that tells you is that 30 applications with no interviews really isn't enough to draw any conclusions from. Once you get to around 50, it starts to look like a pattern, and by the time you're at 100 with nothing to show for it, I would say bad luck isn't a very good explanation anymore.
Now, those figures only matter if the applications you're counting were good to begin with. So before you count an application toward that total, ask yourself a few questions.

The first is whether you were actually qualified for the role. The exercise I usually walk people through is to read the posting from top to bottom and go through the responsibilities and qualifications one by one, putting each one into one of two groups: things you've done before, and things you haven't. By the end, about 70 to 80% of them should be in the first group. If they're not, I wouldn't count that application, because the issue there has more to do with which roles you're going after than with your resume.

The second is timing. A lot of recruiters review applications as they come in and stop once they have enough people to interview, so if you're applying to postings that have been up for four or five weeks, those aren't really a fair test of your resume either.

The last one is whether the job was still open. If the role has been taken down from the company's careers page, it's closed, so leave it out. Ghost jobs are harder to spot. In 2024, Greenhouse found that in any given quarter, somewhere between 18 and 22% of the postings on its platform had no hiring activity behind them, which can include roles that were frozen or cancelled after they went up. A posting that's been up for months or keeps getting reposted is usually a warning sign.
And if you're only counting roles you're qualified for, your real interview rate is probably higher than 3%, which makes a long run of zeros even harder to blame on luck.
If you've sent 50 or more applications that pass all of those checks and you still haven't landed an interview, then there's a good chance your resume is part of the problem.

If you get to that point, I wouldn't start by reformatting. Unless your resume is using graphics, tables, columns, text boxes, or headers and footers, formatting usually isn't what's holding you back. Most of the time, it's more about how the content is written and how it portrays you.

The first place I'd look is the top of the page. Your summary and your most recent role are usually where a recruiter looks first. A quick check I have people do is this: give your resume to a spouse, partner, or friend and have them spend 10 seconds on it. After that, if they still can't put their finger on what you do, there's a good chance a recruiter won't either.

After that, I'd make sure you're using a targeted resume for each type of role you're going for. For example, if you're pursuing business analyst roles but you're also putting your feelers out for project management roles, then you definitely want to be using separate resumes, each one targeted to its own job type.

Then I'd go through your bullet points. Each one should show a skill the job is asking for, and it should be specific enough that it couldn't be pasted into anyone else's resume. Someone outside your team, or even outside your company, should be able to understand it easily, and your most relevant bullets should be near the top of each list.

These are averages across a lot of different industries, so your numbers might look a little different. Tech roles in the Americas are a lot more competitive right now (Ashby saw over 600 inbound applications per hire), while some other fields are a lot easier. Huntr's data is also self-reported by its users, so I'd take that with a grain of salt.
That said, I think having a ballpark is a lot more useful than guessing, and it can help you figure out when it actually makes sense to go back and rework your resume.
